words: No, I don't know if there was any.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, if there was, there was a drug.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We didn't know of it anyway.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I never, I just got those two boys two years between them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then you just never got them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Never got them anymore. Mm-hmm. But I always wanted, that last one that was Martin, I thought, sure, that was going to be a girl. I had named him Beverly Lorraine before he was born.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So then when he got his girl, he named her Beverly Lorraine because that was supposed to be his name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, well, that was nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's how she got the name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you got your granddaughter, even if you didn't get her. Because a lot of women in your age group had large families. Some of them didn't even want so large families.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They sure had big families at the time my mother had her kids. They all had up to 11, 12, and more than that. Yeah. And somebody that had just five or six or something like that, that was, oh, that's awful.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's just the way it was, I guess. Yeah. Okay, let's see. We're down to interest, hobbies, and so forth. I see you do needlework.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, and crocheting. That was...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Is it crocheting? There's no crocheting on that. Is that what the...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Here's Troy in 1891. Oh. And it was called Bulmer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it had a different name then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the Swedes, they got so many Swedes here, they couldn't say Bulmer, they called it for Wilmer. Oh. And then they took and changed it to Troy. Oh. There's in 1891. See, it's stumps on Main Street. Yeah. It was nothing but woods. This whole thing was wild woods. When we went to the...down to Nora there from our place, we went, we had a trail through the woods. Mm-hmm. Nothing but woods.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, because now they've cleared away a lot of it for logging and wheat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now it's all in farmland.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Things change, don't they?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. That's in 1891.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it's here in 19...here's in 1909.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Yeah, it's looking more like a town here, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's improved a lot.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, there's a big difference on this one. Yeah. It's really a pretty town. When we drove out today and looking out... Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we're right down here in the canyon down...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You've always lived in either right outside Troy or in Troy as well your whole life.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Here's in 1920.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Wow, it's really growing, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. And now it's way over...the house is on a hillside. Oh, over.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's probably going to keep growing, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I imagine because they're just keep on building.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Although a lot of people who live in small places don't want them to change now. No. They want them to stay small.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they're just coming in so thick now. Yeah. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay, so you're...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's an interesting book.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I'm going to read it. Okay, so let's see. We've got most of your hobbies down. We've got a big list. Is there any other things that you like to do with your free time?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. I didn't...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You didn't have any free time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, until I started planting flowers and mowing lawn and...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You must be a good cook, too. Cooking all those years and bake, baker.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I guess so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Oh. Yeah. Did you ever have any flowers or anything or any kind of food at the fairs? Did you ever...at the county fairs? No. Uh-huh. I thought you brought anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I never brought anything there because it's too hard to get it there. Yeah. Never got it there. Yeah. I never did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Do you still like to bake or...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. I bake all my bread.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I got a freezer now, so I can put it in the freezer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Yeah, that's nice. Well, homemade bread is a lot better than...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I can't eat that bakery bread. It's just like the more you chew, the bigger it gets. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you belong to...I know you belong to the club that we came to, Dorca Society, or...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I quit all that because I couldn't do anything. But I belong to the church.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And which church?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Adventist Church. Uh-huh. But that's just now later years I've gone back. Because when the first...you know, they sprinkled the kids when baptized the other way? And it was a Swedish Methodist church that stood, oh, probably a mile and a half or something from our place. The house, that church preacher's house is still there. That's Bengals, where Bengal lives now. Uh-huh. And the Swedish Methodist church, and there's where we were baptized. Oh. And then that church died and tore it down. Uh-huh. And then this large club, that was the Nora Mission Church. Oh. And there's where we went to Sunday school, and I was confirmed in that church.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The Mission Church, what church was that affiliated with? Was that Adventist?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, no. Oh. It was a congregational church, something like that. Oh, I see. But they called it the Swedish Mission Church. Uh-huh. And when I was one week old, that church was, they were building it when I was one week old, a week before Thanksgiving. The first meeting in that church was on Thanksgiving when I was a week old.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, my.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that church, that place, that's a good built place. They could move it down here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was it called the Mission Covenant Church?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh, something like that, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's what my husband's family is. Well, then what happened to that church? I mean, I know the church is still there, but what happened to the Mission Church?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It died out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it just didn't go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Go, I guess, and they couldn't have a preacher there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just died out. I see. And then what was left of the members there sold it. I see. Sold to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I see. So when you were a child, you went to the Mission Church. Uh-huh. And then what happened? Then for a period of time you didn't, weren't affiliated with the church?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I don't know. I went to the Lutheran Church and I went to the Nazarene Church, but I never belonged to any of them. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And did your children go to Sunday school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, Raynald was confirmed in the Lutheran Church here, and he went to Sunday school. Well, the kids went to Lutheran all the time. Oh, yeah, uh-huh. And Marvin didn't get confirmed because that class, they were supposed to be confirmed and then the minister told them they'd have to go to spring and the whole class quit. Oh. So he wasn't confirmed. Uh-huh. But Raynald was. Uh-huh. And so they went to that Lutheran. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then how did you get from the Lutheran to the Athens?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. They had some meetings here and just started to talk about it. It was in the Bible. Right. You could see the truth of it. Uh-huh. And that's it. Uh-huh. So then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And when was that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's in 1954.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. So just within the last.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Last few years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Few years, uh-huh. Were you affiliated with the church?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I don't know. I went to the Lutheran Church and I went to the Mastery Church, but I never belonged to any. Uh-huh. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And did your children go to Sunday school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, Raynal was confirmed in the Lutheran Church here. And he went to Sunday school. Well, the kids went to Lutheran all the time. Oh, yeah. Uh-huh. And Marvin didn't get confirmed because that class, they were supposed to be confirmed and then the minister told them they'll have to go until spring and the whole class quit. Oh. So he wasn't confirmed. But Raynal was. And so they went to Lutheran. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then how did you get from the Lutheran to the Adventist?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. They had some meetings here and they started to talk about it. It was in the Bible. Right. You could see the truth of it and that. Uh-huh. So then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And when was that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's in 1954.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. So just within the last.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Last few years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Few years. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, I belonged to the Dorcas. I was Dorcas leader for many years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just, I can't get around anymore so I just kept going.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You did go to the, you were leader of the Dorcas Society. And did you go to any other groups in town when you were younger?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I suppose I went to everything there was. Yeah. To school, you know, there's lots of doings in schools. Oh, sure. When you have school kids.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: PTA and stuff like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the basketball, I never missed the basketball game. And they used to have tournaments here in Troy. And four noon afternoon and evening and I went to all those games. Couldn't stay away from them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. Especially in a little town, basketball is really exciting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, and then Raina played, well, they both did, but football.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Then you wanted me to come to one game. Oh, you can go to one game. So I went to one game and I said, never again. I said, I'm not going to be there when they kill you there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, that's a little more violent than basketball.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, than basketball. That's nice. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, now, were you, you were married in what year? 1920. 1920, so you were married during the Depression years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Depression came later. And we lived in that little house there during the Depression. And there was no work to be gotten. And we had the two kids. We were just starting school. And then they decided they were going to put in the sewer here in Troy. But they'd give them just so many hours a week because there was so much people that wanted to work to make it. And they had just so much money to go on. But then they got food, and all we had to do was go downtown here and get it. We got everything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean? Free. Oh, from the government. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So we was on the relief. And so then we lived there within.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How could you pay your rent?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We did, $6 a month rent and couldn't pay it. He was a bachelor. He didn't need it. He was a rich bachelor anyway.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So he didn't put you out or anything? No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he died. And the house was sold then. So we had lived there for 10 years. But we still owe him $6 a month for several months' rent. But he stabbed them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They didn't need it because they were wealthy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He was a wealthy bachelor.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, how long was it that your husband was not able to find work?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it was, oh, I think it's that summer. He worked in town here, then on the sewer. And then they built these outside toilets and put them in the parks and all of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was the public works, wasn't it? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And anything like that. But they didn't get very much, many hours to do it. Because they had to have just so much money to go on.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then he got the green, had the warehouse there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they wanted somebody to come down there and work. So he went down and started working there. And then he stayed there. And then one day, where Gee Roach lives down there, that was the hospital. Dr. Myers had a hospital there. So one day he came up and he wanted me to come down there and see if I could come down and clean one day. We'd wash clothes one day, wash, clean, wash up. He always took townships on Tuesdays. And he wanted me to come on Monday to clean the whole plane, and Wednesday to wash. So I thought, well, yes, I was glad to go. I went there and worked there. And then we had to move because the house was sold. And I kept on working there. Pretty soon that place got so full of people that I washed almost every day down in that hospital. And I went down after suffering down the ironing and got the clothes out of the way. That place was just packed full. They took townships. They'd come from Elkhorn, from all over. And he had beds in the hall and all over.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, at least they gave you some...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He had a nurse there steady and he had a helper. And they were on there steady. And the women come in there and had their babies there. He operated for pennisitis. That's where my brother died, for ruptured penis. And that place was just full.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that was during the Depression.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: During... yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Glad for the extra money then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. And so then I worked there until... He had two boys. And they grew up and were going to go to some school. And then Mrs. Myers decided she didn't want to stay here any longer. She's going to Seattle. And she took off and the boys took off and left him here alone for a while. So then he sold his house to Jimmy Arnist. Jimmy Arnist lived in that one. He sold it to them and then we rented it. When Jimmy was going to move, we asked to rent that. So we rented it until 45, that's when we bought it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, the World War II, did your husband and son...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Raynold was in World War II, he was in it for four years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And the other one, was he in?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, he didn't pass.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he wasn't in, but Raynold was. He was there in Guadalcanal for just about four years. Around Hawaii.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, that was a hard time too then, wasn't it? During the war. Did you think... which do you think was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know. Then... The Depression was the worst of all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was the worst in the war.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that was the worst of all, because you didn't know what you were going to eat. The kids wanted this and that, and you had to have clothes for them, and they were getting into school, and you didn't know which way to turn. And then, they had this pea-picking in Moscow. I had never done it, I've never seen it, but my sister was working there, and she was getting to be Hopper Wallace, and different things. She said for me to go up there and put my name in and go and pick peas. She said, there's lots of older people than you there picking peas. And so I thought, well... Then it was a whole bunch of us here. We were five or six in the car that went.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And what year was this?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know what year it was.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But during the...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: After the Depression.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: After the Depression, that's what I wondered.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so then we went to picking peas at Washburn and Wilson. And we got on the ship that started work at 3 in the afternoon, and we worked our eight hours in the night. And here it got, I think it was 40 below zero. And we'd come out, and Ida Paulson was driving. It was her car, we loaded with her. Came out there, the car was broke. And we had to go and get help to get that part out. When we got out by the cemetery, the car stopped. And then somebody had stolen the gas.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So we was out of gas. And cars wouldn't stop, they'd just drive by. We couldn't make nobody stop.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it was so cold.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was so cold. They wouldn't stop because maybe they would never get started. Maybe they couldn't get started again some way. And so finally there was one that stopped. And we rode back, a couple of us went with her. And went back and got gas. And then we made it home. And one time going to work, that's where Groblum slid. Now do you know where Groblum slid? It's up there by the... Between here and Moskow. And we was driving down the highway. And here this man comes back and right out of his yard, right back into us.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then Ida Paulson was still driving. We rode with her. And we got to work late. Because we had to get... wait, the police got there. And we had to wait until we got another car to go in and everything. But nobody was hurt. But we went on to work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. Well, in those days you needed every penny too. Yeah. Well...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then we went to work there until I think they closed. They sold out or something. Then Pure Line came in and I worked there. Until 1954. I quit in 1954.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you really worked a great deal in your married life.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yes. And then we had my cup. And where the school bus depot is, is where the my cup plant was. And we cut my cup. We lived in that house then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because a lot of women your age have just stayed home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, but they had to. There was a lot of them working.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They had to, yeah. Because those were all lean years, boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And we cut my cup. That was hard work. Because you had to have it just so. And you had to. You got paid by the way. You couldn't cut off too much either.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, have you enjoyed your leisure since 1954?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What have you enjoyed doing a lot since you haven't had to work? Of course, you've been... you've raised flowers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I... the yard and the mowing and the trimming and the flowers and all that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then you like to cook and to bake and your embroidery.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Usually in the wintertime we'd make things for Christmas. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you ever quilt?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I made so many quilts. Tops. I made... I don't know how. I think I must have made 50 or 60 for the darkest. Because everybody brought pieces. That porch up there was just full of pieces. And so I got... I got hoarse. I got from tearing all those clothes, you know, the pieces. And we sorted clothes to go to the... went there, you know. Yeah. And I got hoarse. So I had to quit all that and I had to go and have surgery in my throat. So I had that sacred heart.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And what did they do?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it was Drury that sent me to Spokane. And when I asked them what was there, they said it was a whole lot of fat in there that never just... never dissolved or anything. It had just plugged up. So when I was talking or reading or something, I had to put my finger in this hole here. Otherwise I couldn't... couldn't hardly talk. So then I had surgery here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When was this? Oh...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not very long ago. About five, six years ago. And I quit all that material and all the quits. I just had to quit it because I was scared of that hoarseness, you know. I could have turned to cancer too. But it wasn't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You seem to be in good health now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Oh, if I had better knees. And so I've made a lot of... Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, what advantages do you think there was to living in a rural community during your childhood? Well, actually your whole life rather than living in the city.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, it was better here at the town and the country. Because then he had to go out and work and I was sitting there alone.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And we had a cow and we had pigs. We had chickens and those things had to be taken care of. So it was better in town.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But what advantages do you think there are to living in a smaller town rather than a big city?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I think it's... you know everybody. And you can go around and you don't have to be scared of anything. Like in big towns, you don't know what happens there. And never think... you can go out any time of night, you know. You don't have to think... even think that anybody would be picking you up.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you know everybody. I used to go down on the street and I knew everybody. Now I don't know anybody. Well, it's all a new people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it's grown.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they're all friendly and nice as far as I know them. I've got acquainted with them. They're all nice people. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Can you think of anything that you and your brothers and sisters used to do for fun when you were children that's different from what the kids do today? Or what kind... can you think of any family experiences when you were a child?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I suppose there's a lot of it. We used to go down the woods and make us playhouses.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, uh-huh. That sounds fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so we used to drag boards down and put them in between the trees and trim off the trees. And broken dishes or whatever, we got a hold of, bring it down. It wasn't too far from the house because the woods was just below there. And then we... we never had any bicycles or anything like that. And there was no water that was up in that country.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You carried your own water.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You carried it, called it for washing. Sometimes we'd go out in the school and do the washing and the barrel was empty. Had to go and get a barrel full of water and heat it before we could wash.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, did you speak Swedish when you were a child?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I started school when I was five years old and I didn't understand the English words.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And how was... what kind of an experience was that? Did the teacher...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And we had an old schoolhouse. The old schoolhouse was on that side of our place. And Berton L. French, you've heard of him. He was my first teacher. I was five years old when I started and we had three months school in the spring and three months in the fall.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, he probably had lots of students, though, didn't he? Yeah. Couldn't speak English. Could he speak any foreign languages? No. Well, how did he teach you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know how he could teach us because as soon as we got outside that door, we all talked Swedish. And they tried to put a stop to it that we couldn't talk Swedish in the school yard. But, see, that didn't work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, because you talked it at home, I suppose.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's all we talked. And that's all we talked between us. That was all we talked. And those American kids, they talked Swedish just as good as we did. The Bostmans and those that went there. Yeah, they learned just as good as we did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you still speak Swedish?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. And I taught my kids to talk Swedish first because if they learn it first, they never forget it. And now, lately, in the store, he can talk Swedish to those people and if they talk to him, he knows what they're talking about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, do you remember, did you learn English then when you were in school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I guess we must have learned it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You must have learned it because that's what you're talking about.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then they were going to build a new schoolhouse and my dad gave them an acre of land up in the corner, the north corner of the place there was an acre. He gave them that. Of course, he got a dollar for it to make it legal. But he gave it to them and they built a new schoolhouse there, Pleasant Hill. And then we went up there to school and I think the first teacher that was there, his name was Blackaby. And we had Steelsmiths live out here on the ridge. Steelsmith was Hazel Trout and Mr. Steelsmith was Benjamin Franklin Steelsmith. He was mean.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then you went, when did you move to Moscow to go to school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's when I was in eighth grade. See, I dropped eighth grade up here. We saw an ad in the Star Mirror that they wanted somebody to work the room and board and go to school, so my folks sent me up there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you went to eighth and ninth grade there?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so we had seats, you know, two could sit in one seat. Oh, right. And they put the first graders down and probably the third graders or something on this, up and down. So the teacher would stand there and teach. And so this girl that I sat with, she was two years older than me. And she had already learned English and she learned what the teacher was talking about. And the teacher said something to me and I didn't know what he said, I didn't understand it. And so she said, at recess, she said, in Swedish of course, that if I don't get up on a stump and keep on turning and turning on that stump, he's going to give me a licking. That's what he told me she said. And I got on that stump. I believed her. The whole recess, 15-minute recess, I went around and around on that stump.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A tree stump you mean?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, a big tree stump where they had cut down a tree.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's funny. That's a funny story. So did you ever find out? How did you find out then?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I never found out. I guess I was mad at her because some of the other kids said that that's what she said. But I found out that it wasn't true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there are a lot of kids from Swedish and Norwegian parents here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you didn't feel out of place? Out of place. They were all Swedes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because in some families or in some areas, you know, they were just all alone and everybody was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you can imagine those poor teachers. We had two young girls. One, her name was Rosa Bore. And she was just a young... You know, they just started teaching when they were 17 years old because they didn't have to go to university. Right. And she was younger than I think some of those school kids. And she would sit there and she'd cry because she didn't know what to do with the kids because they took over, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She couldn't handle them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She couldn't handle them, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she was no good at all to them. They had to get rid of her and they got her sister Rosa Bore out there. Well, she was a little bit better, but she wasn't very good either. The teacher just had to get right down to work to show them that either he gives them a licking or... Because then they could give them a lick. Yeah. And what he did, what Stielschmidt did to them, he took two of the boys. I don't know what they had done, I don't remember. But he stood them up on the floor and they had to spread their legs way apart. And they kept on with their feet until they crawled together and he'd come up there and kick them on the heel until they got their feet. Their legs spread again.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And how long did they have to stay like that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Stay there for half a day at a time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, my.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he just made them stand there. And they all... With penmanship, if you didn't write, I could never learn to make a capital J. I made this tail and then I took them back and made the other half. And they were trying to get me to make that J. And if you couldn't do it, he'd take the pen and he'd stick us on the hands, you know. And it was just awful. You just tried night and day all night and you got home all evening. I tried to make that J.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he sounded a little mean.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think the teacher had to be. Yeah. And we sure learned our lessons.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I guess so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Mrs. Steelsmith was mean too. But they had to be. And then we had one that we liked real well. Her name was the... She was from Avon. But you, Mrs. Butte, she's the one on the picture. Oh, she was good. But the kids liked her and she had control over the kids and she wasn't mean.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's it. I mean, you can have control of the kids and still not be mean.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she was good in a way to them and everything, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they liked her in that and she could handle them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I see your TV. What programs do you like to watch? Do you have any favorites?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. I watch... I used to watch Barker, but he's off now. And I watch Dialing for Dollars. I don't watch very much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't have any real favorites?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. As the world turns, it's the only one that I watch that's really interesting. I never start any of those stories. Because I don't want to be panned out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But As the World Turns comes on at 12.30 and he's off at 1.30 and it just gives me time I can lay on the Davenport. But I sleep half of the time, so I don't know sometimes what's been going on. Yeah. But anyway, I don't have anything in particular. And I'm not so awful on the television. I just don't have... just radio.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you read?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. I read.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you like to read?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. I've been reading... these church papers that come and...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: come and...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's a good one. I don't know where that comes from. It's different magazines that I get. I don't think that's an Adventist paper. It's some other, but it's a good reading. So I don't know. I don't read any of these continuous stories or anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How do you think life for your granddaughter or grandchildren will be different from what... the kind of life you've led? How do you think times have changed for their...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, the way it looks for my granddaughter, that it's getting just as bad as it was in the early days. Because he's logging. He's working with logging up in Troy, Montana, and she lives up there. And they use a coal oil lamp. And she's way out of... it's many miles out of Troy, Montana. And in the woods she lives in a shack there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Doesn't have a lot of modern conveniences.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so the way she's starting out, I think she'll be worse off than I am.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I mean, generally, do you think that the young people now will have a harder life?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. It's harder in a way because they just can't get any work. Then it was work. After the Depression was over, it got work. And it seems like it's been work ever since. It hasn't been too hard. But now they have put in so much machinery. That takes the place of men and people. So there's no work. So it's harder in a way on account of all that. But I think they get more education.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh my. Was this in the paper then, these two pictures? Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They were both in the paper. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Who made the decisions, or how did you arrive at decision-making in your marriage?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know. I suppose I maybe made the most of them because he was on the quiet side. So I think probably that I was the...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The stronger one?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Strong, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, do you think it was easier then, or in some ways, for him to have gone first if you were the stronger one? Do you think it would have been harder for him?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I was so scared I was going to die first. Because he could never have taken care of himself. He was just about helpless. Oh, I was so scared that I was going to... When I got that throat trouble, I was so scared that I was going to go... That it was cancer or something, and I died before him because he... So when he was leaving, it was... Afterwards, I thought, well, it was sure good he died first.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean helpless in what way? You mean that he couldn't...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, he couldn't decide anything, and I don't know, he was just... Of course, he was getting old. He was 84.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he was older than you. Yeah. What do you think attracted you to him when you were courting?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it was up there at the camp, at the...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is that where you met him, at a logging camp? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I was cooking there, and he'd come in, and the girl that cooked with me there, she... The boss was her boyfriend. She had... That was her boyfriend. And he'd come in, and then Wofford'd come in, too, and wash dishes while they'd take the dish towel, dry the dishes. And I guess that kind of started it. But Wofford had a girlfriend in Deary, so on weekends, he'd go to Deary. Oh. And so then, I never thought about it much. So then one Sunday evening, we was going to drive down to church. And I was in a sled and horses.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, my.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And we was going to go, and so they asked me if I wanted this... My girlfriend's there, her boyfriend, asked if I wanted... He named a certain guy out there, cook house... In the bunkhouse. And I said, no, I didn't want him. I said, I'll just go with you. And so then when we come... Go driving up from the mill up to the road, we met Wofford. He was coming back from Deary. He stopped, and he asked him if he wanted to go along. When he asked me first if we'd meet Wofford up in here, should we ask him if he wants to go along, I said, yeah. And so we met him there. He got in, and oh, he went to Deary a couple more times, and then he quit going there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He decided not to go there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I guess so, or something. And anyway, he'd come in, and in the evenings, he'd come in, and they'd sit inside and talk to us. And that's how it got started, I guess. It just kept on going that way.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you think you liked about him?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, he was awfully quiet, and he was nice. And I don't know, something, I don't know. And then he went to the war.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was nice looking. He's a nice picture. He seems to be nice looking. Then did you correspond and write letters during the war?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. All the time when he was in the army.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That must have been hard, too, not knowing if he was going to come back or not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, we didn't know. So many didn't have hardly any training, and just sent them over there and killed them. But he came back, and then we started working again, and kept on. Two years more. So 1920 in the fall.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then that's when you got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They always teased me that that was sleep gear.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Catch a man, huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I got the man in Leapy. So, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Can you think of anything else that you might think of, or anything that you can think of that you might tell? Say, if a young woman was going to move to a little town like Troy, any advice you might give her about coming to a small town to live?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think if they have kids, they should go to a small town, because they can, not like here, they can walk up to the schoolhouse, and then as soon as they get out of school, they can just run home. And so it's better to be in a little place like this with kids. And there's no danger of anybody picking them up. You can feel safe that no harm comes to them. If it would, it sure would be a surprise. But we were surprised too when the bank was robbed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, was your bank robbed?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it was robbed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, my.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They locked up Rocky in the back and robbed the bank.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, my. Did they catch them?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, they got them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So, anything else you can think of about your life as a rural woman?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It sounds, what do you think about work in these present days? It sounds like you had your share.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've worked all my life, so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What's your attitude or viewpoint about work?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know. You work, but you've got something to do, and you're more satisfied.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you think that people look differently on work now than they did when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, now it seems like they just leave their kids babysitters, and that's because they just want to work. But everything is so high, and they pretty much have to if they're going to make it. But they never stay home with their babies. They have the babies, and probably in a month they go to work and have a babysitter. Well, they don't know what it is to raise their kids.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, when you had your baby, you were home with them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But then you did work.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I worked, but then they were in school then, and I just went during the day.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I see. You were always home before they went to school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was home before them, and at the same time, anyway. And then when I went to cutting the mica and picking peas there, well, then they were big, so they could take care of themselves.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, what do you see happening to the children when the mothers go off to work like that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think they get so spoiled that they just won't be able to live with them. Because when the mothers come home, they just spoil them. So terrible. And then with the babysitter, she lets them have their way. And I think the kids just get ruined. You can see it on some of these ten-year-old kids. Nine, ten-year-old kids. They just boil rotten. If they don't get their way, why, they just sit there and pout.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you think that parents aren't as strict as they were when you were a parent?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. Teachers aren't either, because then they could lick them, give them a lick, and the rest of us would get scared of them, and we'd try to do better. Now it's against the law. I don't think the parents are even allowed to lick the kids, give them a lick, now because they say they beat them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, well, at least you can spank them, but just not beat them, black them, blue them, something. But of course, back then it was different. They could take them back behind the bar. Do you think you were pretty strict with your boys? They knew who was boss.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I tried to be, but you can't for a while, but then pretty soon they get too old for that, too. So then they go and do sick leave. So it's an end to that, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You get them the first few years, then you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, until they're through the grades in school. When they get into high school, it's a big change. Because then they just... it just changed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, they're reaching adolescence, you know, and then they think they know what's best.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But during the eighth grades in school, I didn't know that they could control them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think the parents get their chance, you know, the first eight years, the first eight grades, and then after that they hope they've done the right thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I think that the kids should... really, the first six years of their life is when they get their start. And I think the mothers should be home with the kids and not be working like they do now. But I don't think you can hardly find a place now where the mother stays home with her baby.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I suppose a lot of, like you say, a lot of people feel they have to if they want to feed them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it costs them much if they're renting or if they're buying. They buy a house, they have to have the payments and all that other expenses. If they rent, the rent is so terrible high. That's different than $6 a month you couldn't pay to them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when you were a child, and you were the oldest child, how did you find being the oldest child? Did you find that hard? Did you have to work a lot harder?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yeah, it was hard. It was hard. And I got blamed for things that they do, you know. And they got out of it. And I was supposed to look after them and see that they did the right thing. Otherwise I'd get it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you have to work pretty hard?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yeah. I was seven years old when my oldest brother there was born. And she had already had us three girls and then he was the next. He was the fourth one. And my dad showed me, well I had to set the bread. He helped me to set the bread. And then he told me when the bread got raced up, I should take pieces of it and put it in a pan, you know. I knew that because I've seen my mother do it. But I could never shape them. I just could not get them little shapes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And you were only seven years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I was seven years old then and she was laying in bed and had him. And then he said I should keep firing the stove. Well I had to, of course she'd holler at me and tell me to do this and do that. And I tell you it's hard to be the oldest one. Yeah, I think so. You have a lot of responsibilities. And they expect an awful lot out of the, and the kids, they're really mean to the oldest one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because they can do things and then they just say no, she did it. It's her fault.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you had to do a lot of chores and work around the house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yeah, all the chores. So when we'd come home from school, I went right to the barn, cleaned the barn, put hay in the mangers and got the cows in.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you milk too?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did that part. My sister started peeling potatoes and cooked the supper. Because she stayed in and I went out. So we had that to do after school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Were all the children pretty close together? Oh yeah. Do you think your mother wanted to have that large of a family?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think so, but I guess they didn't know what to do, they just got them. But she lived to be almost 99 years old. So it didn't hurt her any.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it sure didn't, did it? But yeah, because even in your generation they didn't have as many children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, no they didn't. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wonder how they prevented themselves from having so many kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know. I don't know how they did, but they just didn't get them. Oh, I would have liked to have kept them until I had a grandmother, but then I got it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and nowadays too most people don't have as many kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, they don't have so many now. But I think they're getting ahead more though than they used to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, do you think so?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know. It seems like they have, I know there's a family that comes, they had some meetings here in the Grange Hall on Sunday, and I think they have five little ones, she leads one and he carries one, and then the others. So it looks like they're getting bigger families again. So I don't know, but it sure costs an awful lot of money to raise them, because their shoes and clothes are so expensive.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And back in your days, I think, didn't people make do more? I mean, like you sewed and you canned and you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They don't have time for it now because they work. And I don't think any of these younger married women do any canning, because they don't have time, because they're working, they've got to keep their job.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you sew your clothes even until, once you got older?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When I went to the, I was going to go to the camps and that's where I sewed my dresses, my clothes to take with me.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What about since you were married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yeah, I did all the time, until just now, the later year.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well let me see if there's anything I, can you think of anything that might be interesting about your early life or middle life?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'll look and see if I, I'll turn this off. When you had your boys, what did you do as a family for any recreation, was there any time for that sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well we, we bought us an old model T-Force, the cars come, a model T-Force, and we'd ride around the country, you know, and drive around and we'd go out in the woods. And we'd go huckleberry picking, go on Saturday night, stay overnight, sleep on the ground and go pick huckleberries.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you have a tent or?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, we slept right in the open.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you make pies?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh yeah, pan them, got a lot of huckleberries.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you used to go on picnics or fish or things like that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, as long as, and then took and traded that, well that model T-Force, he just got too old. And we traded him off for a homemade radio.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh my, so then you could listen to things at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that radio runs yet. Does we have a stop here, not very long? I got you. Somebody else's, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean like old things you had?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, well it was old, everything that I didn't want anymore, all kinds of junk. And I sold the wood stove. It's been sitting there in that basement for many years there. I think it was there when we come there. And I got $105 for it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was going to say, a lot of those old things are really worth quite a bit of money.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I was up in the house and I'd open the door and the basement was just full of people. Because it stood there and they just let them buy it right in the basement. And I heard a baby and I thought, oh no, and that stove is rusty. I tried to clean it off but I couldn't get all the rust off. And I thought, oh, that's terrible. And I got nervous over it. But they all were going so high priced.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well that's the way it is with older things. When my grandma died, my mother's people, you know, they all had a sale. And she says now, I sometimes wish I wouldn't have let so many things go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, because things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it's just this last year now that those sales have come in. Now when my mother left her house over there, she lived two years in my apartment basement there. Before we took her to the nursing home. Then they didn't have sales. And we let the second hand man come up and pick out what he wanted. And then what he didn't want, that was it. Because nobody wanted to buy it then. It's just this last year they have started in buying this antique stuff and old stuff.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's really pretty.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now that belongs to the house here. But I had glasses in there. I had them in a box. And then I took them to the sale.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I thought I had methanol. And I took the five to the sale. And I was going to keep the six. When I came home I took them out of the box. And I thought if those were six dollars a piece, they're going to sit up in here. I got six dollars a piece.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I got thirty dollars for five. They're beautiful. They're heavy. I wonder where they were made. Boy they're pretty. Were they a wedding present?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, not these. No I didn't sell any of the wedding presents. I'm not going to drag on a dozen of these.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, because I've got plenty here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I've got a lot of my wedding presents left. Here's our gold wedding ring.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Here's one more of our gold wedding rings.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you have a celebration every year?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, just in the Grange Hall. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What did you, have you found the biggest adjustment to be alone after being married to someone so long?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh I don't know. It just goes day after day. Now that's my sister's. They're my sister's only child that she had. And they got all those boys.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My goodness, six.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Six of them and they're twins. Two of them is twins. And so then when the last, when she's going to have the last one, we said it's just got to be a girl. And there it was Ginny.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Another boy. So she had six, they had six of them. And the twins, one twin is going to school in Moscow. And he's been in the Navy and he's getting his schooling. And his wife goes to school too. And the other twin is in the Coast Guard, the National Guard, something down on the coast. And he is married. And one of the boys is married and lives in Spokane and he has two boys. And then one goes to school in Nampa. He's there. And one is going to college, Gonzaga College. And the other one is finishing high school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is that your boy during the war? Yeah. Yeah, he's a nice looking boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's during the war. That's taken from the water canal.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is he the one that was hurt?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, no, this is the one that's in Rosario store. And he looks just like that. If you ever go in Rosario store, you just can't miss him because he's... He looks just like, he never changed. And he's 54. And that's my mother up there, that was in the paper. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When you got married, what did the girls expect from marriage then? Did they just expect that they would get married and have a bunch of children and stay home?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know what they could expect.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you know what you expected or what your expected?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I expected there'd be a house full of kids. Because I figured that it would go just like it did at home, there wasn't so many. And I didn't want that many. I didn't want kids.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A lot of times the oldest one, you have to take care of so many younger ones.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it's so sick and tired of them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That when you get married, then you don't want to have children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the three youngest ones at home were boys, and I said, I sure don't want any boys. And then I got two of them. So, I had sense enough to quit, I guess. Because I didn't have six anyway.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, right. Sometimes that happens. She could have more and they could still be boys.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But six, that was enough.
